'''''Ruta chalepensis''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Rutaceae]] family known by the common name '''fringed rue'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUCH4|taxon=Ruta chalepensis|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> It is native to the Mediterranean and is found elsewhere as an [[introduced species]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:775070-1|access-date=21 June 2023|title=Ruta chalepensis|work=Kew Plants of the World Online}}, distribution map.</ref>  It is a perennial herb growing up to 80 centimeters tall. The leaves are compound, each divided into several segments which are subdivided into smaller leaflets. The [[inflorescence]] is a cluster of flowers, each with four or five bright yellow petals with rolled, fringed edges. The fruit is a textured capsule which is divided into pointed lobes.

In [[herbalism|traditional herbal medicine]], the plant is used for a number of ailments, such as [[fever]] and [[inflammation]].<ref>al-Said, M. S., et al. (1990). Studies on ''Ruta chalepensis'', an ancient medicinal herb still used in traditional medicine. ''Journal of Ethnopharmacology'' 28:3 305-12.</ref>

''R. chalepensis'' is the original source of the chemical compound [[chalepensin]].<ref>{{cite journal | title = Chalepensin, chalepin, and chalepin acetate, three novel furocoumarins from ruta chalepensis | author = Brooker, Robert M.; Eble, John N.; Starkovsky, Nicolas A. | journal = Lloydia | date = 1967 | volume = 30 | issue = 1 | pages = 73–77 }}</ref>

==Culinary==
''R. chalepensis'' is an introduced species in Ethiopia, where it is cultivated in gardens in almost every province of the country and used as a culinary herb.  The seeds are used to flavour [[Wat (food)|wats]] and the leaves as a condiment in coffee and tea.<ref>{{cite book|last=Goettsch|first=E.|year=1991|chapter=Spice germplasm in Ethiopia|title=Plant Genetic Resources of Ethiopia|editor-last1=Engels|editor-last2=Hawkes|editor-last3=Worede|editor-first1=J.M.M.|editor-first2=J.G.|editor-first3=Melaku|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0-521-384567}}, p.128.</ref>  Called ''Tena adam'' (Adam's health) in [[Amharic]], it is used in the [[Coffee ceremony of Ethiopia and Eritrea|Ethiopian coffee ceremony]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Egata|last2=Gosa|first1=Desta Fikadu|first2=Aynalem|year=2020|title=Ethiopian Rue (Ruta chalapensis L.) Genotypes Morphological and Biological Performance at Different Locations of Southern Ethiopia|journal=Medicinal Chemistry <!---Please do not remove this under the Predatory Journals concept: it may be one, but it is reliable enough for the limited proposition for which it is cited.--->|volume=10|issue=10|pages=1–5|doi=10.37421/mccr.2020.10.565|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}.</ref>  Its dried fruit are marketed as a spice in Western countries, often under the name "passion berries" since the odour is said to resemble [[passion fruit]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.depeperwinkel.nl/en/products/tena-adam|access-date=21 June 2023|title=Tena'adam|work=Deperwinkel|year=2023}}.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.souschef.co.uk/products/terre-exotique-passion-berry-25g|access-date=21 June 2023|title=Terre Exotique Passion Berry 25g|work=Sous Chef}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://steenbergs.co.uk/passion-berry-standard-jar-20g-pas021|title=Passion Berry standard jar|work=Steenbergs}}.</ref>
